item.title: Why Adults Still Like Stickers
item.description:
Motivation

Why Adults Still Like Stickers

Small rewards can make invisible effort feel real.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Small rewards can make delayed adult goals feel immediate and visible.
  • Stickers can support autonomy, competence, and social connection.
  • A sticker can become evidence that invisible effort still counts.

I am an adult, and I am proud to admit that I am currently in the midst of completing two “sticker challenges”—one at my gym and another at the library. The rules are simple: Show up for class or read a book, and paste a sticker down on a bingo square. Each completed “bingo” is a raffle ticket for a prize, and a full “perfect bingo” puts you in the drawing for an even more special one.

Now, if I am to be quite honest with myself, it appears to me that the stickers are what motivate me more than the final reward itself. I know that winning a raffle is very unlikely, even with multiple entries, but a sticker is a simple, tangible, visible reinforcement of the fact that I showed up and took a challenging workout class, or finished a book. And sometimes that is all it takes.

This is, on the surface of it, a slightly embarrassing thing to admit. Adults are supposed to be motivated by loftier things: health, discipline, intellectual enrichment, personal growth, and perhaps a deep commitment to becoming the best version of oneself. And yet, here I am, arranging my week so that I can earn a sticker.

What Makes Stickers So Effective?

Perhaps a sticker is rarely just a sticker.

For adults, small rewards can compress several motivational signals into one tiny object: I made progress. It is noticeable. I belong here. I can do this. The prize is uncertain and distant. The sticker is immediate and definite.

Self-determination theory, one of the most influential theories of human motivation, suggests that people are more likely to stay motivated when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Autonomy is the feeling that we are choosing what we do, competence is the feeling that we are improving, and relatedness is the feeling that we are connected to other people.

A sticker challenge can, surprisingly enough, meet all three needs. I choose to attend the workout class or read the book, so there is autonomy. The sticker provides evidence that I have completed one more step, so there is competence. And because other people are participating in the same challenge, there is relatedness, too. We are all, in some small and slightly silly way, doing this together.

This might explain why badges, progress bars, and streaks are everywhere now. Fitness apps congratulate us for moving. Language apps celebrate our streaks. Coffee shops reward us with stars. We may not always call these things stickers, but psychologically, many of them do the same work. They make progress visible.

And visibility matters because so many adult goals are invisible while we are in the middle of pursuing them. We do not become healthier after one workout. We do not become well-read after one book. We do not become calmer after one meditation session. Adult life is full of effort whose rewards are delayed, ambiguous, or impossible to measure in the moment.

The sticker, then, is not the real reward. It is a tiny piece of evidence.

A sticker chart converts an abstract process into something concrete. I can look at the bingo square and say, “There. I did that.” The larger goal may be months away, but the sticker arrives now. And the human brain seems to like such immediate signals.

Potential Downsides of Small Rewards

Of course, not all rewards are created equal. A sticker can motivate, but it can also annoy. A badge can feel encouraging, but it can also feel manipulative. The difference may lie in whether the reward feels like acknowledgment or control.

If I were forced to attend a class and then handed a sticker in a tone that suggested I should be grateful for it, I suspect I would suddenly become much less fond of stickers. This is the tricky thing about extrinsic rewards: They work best when they support our internal motivation rather than replace it.

The reward itself may matter less than the story we attach to it. A dollar given as a bonus might feel insulting. A handwritten note might make someone’s week. A cheap sticker from a beloved teacher, trainer, librarian, therapist, or friend might carry more emotional weight than a more expensive but impersonal prize.

The Meaning Behind a Reward

Perhaps we should not be so quick to dismiss these small forms of motivation as childish. The adult world often asks us to keep going without much acknowledgment. We send emails, meet deadlines, care for children, exercise, cook, clean, pay bills, manage relationships, all with very few gold stars along the way.

No wonder a sticker feels good.

The challenge, then, is not to eliminate small rewards from adult life in the name of maturity. A good small reward should not make us feel controlled, or dependent on praise for every action. It should function as a marker, a nudge, a visible sign of invisible effort.

I do not know whether I will win either raffle. Statistically speaking, probably not. But I do know that I have gone to classes I might otherwise have skipped, and read books that might otherwise have sat in a pile by my bedside, making me feel vaguely guilty. And I know that each sticker has given me a small, almost absurd amount of satisfaction.

Maybe the reason adults still like stickers is not that we never grew up. Maybe it is that grown-up life gives us too few visible signs that our effort counts.

item.title: Our Brains and Bodies on Meditation
item.description:
Meditation

Our Brains and Bodies on Meditation

Recent research expands our knowledge of the positive effects of meditation.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • The goal of meditation is to calm the mind.
  • Evidence of the positive impacts of meditation continues to grow.
  • Recent studies underscore the value of a daily meditation practice.

When it comes to meditation, the more we learn, the more compelling the case for establishing a meditation practice becomes. A meditation practice essentially allows us, for a prescribed period of time, to turn our attention away from the outer world and focus inward, in silence. While there are many types of meditation, the goal of meditation is to calm the mind.

The scientifically proven benefits of meditation are many and varied. Mental health benefits include reduced stress, depression, and anxiety; improved attention, memory, and focus; and a greater sense of calm. Physical benefits include lower cortisol levels, which lead to improvements in heart rate and blood pressure, rest, and digestion, and pain reduction. What’s more, a meditation practice also enhances our ability to process emotions, enabling us to respond with compassion rather than react to challenging events and situations.

Recent Research on Meditation

Despite the thousands of research studies on the benefits of meditation, researchers continue to study its mechanisms, benefits, and effects on our physical and mental health. Two recently published research studies add to the compelling case for establishing a daily meditation practice.

A recently published international study led by Université de Montréal psychology professor and Canada Research Chair in Computational Neuroscience and Cognitive Neuroimaging, Karim Jerbi, PhD, examined the brains of 12 monks while engaged in meditation using advanced neuroimaging technology. They found that meditation produced a profound increase in the complexity of brain activity in these subjects. In a Université de Montréal UdeMnouvelles article on the study’s research findings, Jerbi described meditation as “…an active state that engages attentional processes [that] affects several aspects of brain function, leading to improved well-being and a reduction in stress and symptoms of anxiety and depression.”

Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, in a 2025 study, shared their findings on the profound changes in both brain activity and physiology in participants following a single intensive week-long residential retreat that included 33 hours of guided meditation, supportive mind/body practices, and lectures. The study reported numerous brain and metabolic changes, as evidenced by brain scans and blood chemistry, including enhanced neuroplasticity, improved metabolic flexibility, and a rise in endogenous opioid levels (the body's natural painkiller) at the conclusion of the retreat.

These two studies add to the thousands of published scientific research findings that make a compelling case for initiating a daily meditation practice. The question becomes: How can we move from meditation-curious to establishing a serious daily meditation practice?

From Curious to Serious

Renowned meditation teacher Reverend Mark Thomas, in an interview on my psychology podcast, A Deeper Podcast, extolled the benefits of a daily meditation practice, describing it as a “deep quiet that each of us has, but does not often have the opportunity to visit … and that people who meditate hang out there a lot.”

Thomas has dedicated his life to helping others transition from being meditation-curious to establishing a serious, committed meditation practice. He describes a daily meditation practice as a means of “dropping into that silence, which enables the practitioner to bring that with them into their day.” A daily practice, he says, mitigates stress, eliminates fatigue, helps you manage relationships, and find a clear direction in life. “These,” he says, “are just some of the benefits of a daily meditation practice.

To begin a meditation practice, Thomas suggests seeking outside help and finding a practice that feels genuine to you. He stresses the importance of establishing a practice that fits your lifestyle, preferences, and daily routines. As for his best piece of advice about meditation, Thomas says: “Don’t judge it while you’re in the midst of a meditation. The biggest benefits of meditation are experienced outside of the meditative bubble. Meditation will cause a positive ripple effect in your life, and in your world.”

6 Strategies to Help Kick-start a Daily Meditation Practice

  1. Start simple. When beginning your meditation practice, it is important to set realistic, simple, achievable goals. Set aside a few minutes each day, when and where you will not be interrupted.

  2. Get comfortable. Meditation is a practice, not a punishment. Finding a comfortable position with help support a daily practice you will look forward to with positivity. Begin by turning your attention to your breath.

  3. Acknowledge and release thoughts when they arise. Try to be patient rather than frustrated or disappointed when thoughts show up. Learning to let go of intrusive thoughts is a valuable part of establishing a meditation practice.

  4. Resist the urge to judge or label your meditation experience. Many novice meditators become discouraged when they don’t feel an immediate in-the-moment benefit. Bear in mind that the benefits of meditation play out in virtually every aspect of your life, not necessarily and certainly not exclusively while you're meditating.

  5. Reflect on the positive changes you begin to experience in your daily life. This includes better sleep, an enhanced ability to focus, and the ability to deal with difficult or changing situations and events.

  6. Seek out resources to enhance your meditation practice when you feel ready. A meditation teacher, a group, a meditation app, a book, or a course on meditation are among the many and varied resources easy to find and readily available.

item.title: If I Can’t Have It, Neither Can You: Exploring Crab Mentality
item.description:
Jealousy

If I Can’t Have It, Neither Can You: Exploring Crab Mentality

Crab mentality can turn milestones into moments of sabotage.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • When family members respond to success with jealousy, minimization, or sabotage, it's called "crab mentality."
  • Crab mentality is often driven by insecurity, scarcity thinking, and fear of change.
  • Boundaries, selective sharing, and supportive relationships can help protect one's sense of peace.
Source: AI Generated

In toxic families, “crab mentality” occurs when relatives sabotage or undermine your success out of jealousy, fear, or insecurity. Although this behavior can occur in the workplace, in higher education, and in friendships, it can feel especially painful when it happens within families.

The phrase comes from the image of crabs in a bucket, pulling one another down when one tries to escape. In families, this can look like relatives discouraging your goals, minimizing your achievements, or making you feel guilty for growing beyond the roles they expected you to stay in.

Social comparison theory helps explain part of this dynamic. People regularly look to others to determine their perceived worth. Upward comparisons cause feelings of insecurity, whereas downward comparisons elicit temporary feelings of superiority. When a family member’s success highlights another person’s insecurity, stagnation, or regret, that success may feel threatening rather than inspiring.

In healthy family systems, people generally celebrate one another’s growth. They cooperate, encourage, and take pride in shared success. In toxic systems, however, one person’s advancement may be treated as betrayal, rejection, or proof that someone else has fallen behind.

Milestones such as educational advancement, marriage, a new job, a new home, or financial stability can all trigger this kind of reaction.

How Crab Mentality Manifests in Toxic Families

Sometimes the sabotage is subtle. A family member may sulk in the corner during your graduation celebration, refuse to acknowledge your accomplishment, or change the subject when others praise you.

Other times, the behavior is more overt. They may create conflict at your wedding, criticize your parenting, insult your career path, or behave disruptively during an event that should have centered your joy.

They may minimize your achievement by attributing your success to luck rather than effort. Statements such as “You get everything you want” ignore the discipline, sacrifice, and persistence that likely made the achievement possible.

They may also use guilt to pull you back into old family norms. Comments like “You think you’re better than us now” often say more about their insecurity than your actual behavior.

In my book, (dis)Honor Thy Mother: Daughterhood, Dysfunction, and Deliverance, I describe several examples of this dynamic, including experiences around graduation, marriage, and parenting. One particularly painful example occurred at my farewell party before I left for my doctoral program. While I was already struggling with impostor feelings as the first person in my family to go to college, my mother told me, “I cannot see you being any good at that anyway.”

That kind of comment is not simply “being honest.” It is an attempt to plant doubt at a moment when support is needed most.

What Drives Crab Mentality

Insecurity is often the primary driver of the crab mentality. Tearing someone else down can become a coping mechanism for people who feel inadequate, left behind, or threatened by another person’s growth.

Scarcity thinking also plays a role. Some relatives believe there is only room for one person to rise, succeed, or be celebrated. Instead of seeing one family member’s success as a collective win, they experience it as a personal loss.

Change can also disrupt the family equilibrium. When one person heals, grows, earns more, leaves, marries, or creates a healthier life, the family system may no longer function in the same familiar way. Even positive change can feel threatening to people invested in keeping old roles intact.

Fear of abandonment may also be present. Some family members worry that your education, career, relationships, or new lifestyle will cause you to leave them behind emotionally, physically, or socially. Rather than naming that fear directly, they may criticize your growth.

Learning to Spot Crab Mentality

Crab mentality often shows up in language. Listen for words that shrink your accomplishment: “little,” “easy,” “lucky,” “small,” or “not a big deal.”

It can also show up in behavior. A relative may miss important events, arrive late, show little enthusiasm, refuse to congratulate you, or bring up past mistakes when you are being celebrated.

Another sign is resentment without effort. Some people are not asking how to grow, improve, or create change in their own lives. They simply resent that you did.

How to Protect Yourself

  • Set firm boundaries. You can clearly communicate what behavior is unacceptable without being drawn into a debate. For example, you might say, “I am not discussing my accomplishments if they are going to be minimized,” or “If this conversation becomes insulting, I am going to end it.”
  • Use an information diet. This means limiting how much access certain people have to your private life. You may choose to share less about your finances, relationships, goals, parenting, or career plans with people who consistently use that information to criticize or undermine you.
  • Find your support system. Even in toxic families, there may be one person who genuinely celebrates you. If not, look outside the family. Friends, mentors, colleagues, chosen family, therapists, faith communities, or support groups can offer the encouragement your family may not be able to provide.

You are allowed to grow, succeed, and build a life that looks different from the one you came from. Other people’s discomfort with your growth does not mean you are doing something wrong. Sometimes it means you are finally moving toward freedom.

item.title: Do Controlling Parents Create Agresssive Children?
item.description:
Parenting

Do Controlling Parents Create Agresssive Children?

Netflix crime documentary "What Jennifer Did" highlights her strict upbringing.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Netflix documentary "What Jennifer Did" raises the question: Do controlling parents cause aggression?
  • Past research has identified a parenting style called guan common in Asian households.
  • Guan emphasizes hard work and self-discipline.
  • A 2015 study found that parenting control, more than guan, was associated with aggressive action.

This post was conceived by and co-written with Joshua Youngwood, Rose-Hulman class of 2027. It was edited by Stephanie Youngwood.

"What Jennifer Did"
Source: Netflix / 2024

The 2024 Netflix true-crime documentary, What Jennifer Did, tells the story of then 24-year-old Jennifer Pan, who was convicted of first-degree murder for hiring hitmen to kill her parents. Jennifer’s mother, Bich, was killed, but her father, Hann, survived the attack. During the investigation, the history of the Pan family’s relationship was revealed. Bich and Hann were Vietnamese immigrants who raised Jennifer and her younger brother, Felix, in a very strict household. Her parents had high expectations and closely monitored how she spent her free time. By age four, Jennifer was already enrolled in piano lessons. Over time, she became overwhelmed by her parents’ expectations. She began lying to them about attending the University of Toronto, even forging report cards and student loan documents. When her parents discovered her lies, she and her boyfriend, Daniel Chi-Kwong Wong, hired hitmen to kill them in a staged robbery.

While the documentary highlights Daniel’s past criminal involvement as a major catalyst for the violent and tragic outcomes, it raises questions about Jennifer’s relationship with her controlling parents and the differences between Western and Asian parenting.

Controlling or disciplined?

Bich and Hann followed an approach known as “authoritarian” or “tiger" parenting, defined by high expectations and restrictions for children, with limited warmth. Interestingly, initial research comparing Asian and Caucasian children under authoritarian parenting styles found that Asian children tended to report higher achievement and less stress than Caucasian children. Psychologists then experimented with different parenting techniques to explain these findings, and three aspects were assigned to better describe Asian parenting: warmth, control, and guan. Warmth pertains to love and understanding, control is defined by high demands and a hostile or distant relationship, and guan refers to nurturing children by encouraging self-discipline and hard work.

Warmth, control, and guan: How they relate to aggression

A 2015 study by Yu Gao, Wei Zhang, and Annis Lai Chu Fung sought to further understand the relationship between parenting styles and children’s aggression types. Specifically, they wanted to examine how the three aspects correlated with two types of aggression: reactive aggression and proactive aggression. Reactive aggression refers to negative behavior in response to provocation, while proactive aggression is taking preemptive actions for personal gain. The study collected data from over 4000 Hong Kong schoolchildren from 12 primary and 11 secondary schools. The children were given a Reactive–Proactive Aggression Questionnaire (RPQ) to assess their perception of their aggression, while their parents were given a Parenting Inventory and an RPQ to assess their perception of their parenting style and their child’s aggression type.

The RPQs evaluated aggression by asking how much the children “reacted angrily when provoked by others” (reactive aggression) and “hurt others to win a game” (proactive aggression). The Parenting Inventory asked parents to rate agreement with statements like “I am restrictive/controlling of my child.”

The researchers first found that guan was negatively correlated with rated proactive aggression from both boys and girls; for boys, warmth was also negatively correlated with proactive aggression. Guan was positively correlated with reactive aggression from boys and girls. Finally, parenting styles with high control were associated with high reactive aggression in boys and girls, and controlling parents reported higher proactive aggression for boys. These findings suggest that even though guan has been associated with high achievement, it may have some costs.

Study limitations

The study had several limitations. Crucially, perceptions were not measured over time, so researchers could not draw a causal relationship between parenting style and aggression. For example, they couldn’t tell if an aggressive child resulted in a more controlling parent or the other way around. The study also relied on self-reported data, which is susceptible to biases. For example, it might be difficult for a parent to admit to employing a harsher parenting style.

Could Jennifer Pan’s controlling parents and strict upbringing have led her to wanting to kill her parents? The study by Gao et al. suggests that parenting styles are linked to aggression. But any link is surely far from direct. For starters, lots of children have controlling parents, but outcomes like Jennifer’s are exceptionally rare.

item.title: How the Father Complex Shapes the "Tradwife" Movement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How the Father Complex Shapes the "Tradwife" Movement

The father complex influences our relationship to authority.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • How a person experiences their father and other authority figures is often shaped by the father complex.
  • Strong reactions to issues of authority, achievement, and power often reveal an activated father complex.
  • Complexes aren't eliminated; they become less activated through conscious reflection and choice.

It’s a timeless topic that perennially gets a new spin: power and authority. We have opinions about who has it, who doesn’t, and why that matters. In Carl Jung’s psychology, power, achievement, and authority figures are often associated in the psyche with the father, patriarchy, and masculine, which are all associated with the proverbial father complex.

Carl Jung described complexes as emotionally charged bundles of memories and experiences—“feeling-toned groups of representations”—that cluster together and organize around a core theme or archetype such as “father,” “mother,” or “attachment.”

Complexes are shaped through early and ongoing personal, relational, and cultural experiences. They influence how we think, feel, and respond, and can congeal into enduring response patterns. You can read more about complexes here and the mother complex here.

In my last post, I covered ten characteristics of complexes that I first learned from Jungian psychoanalyst Dr. Florence Irvine, such as “having a life of their own,” strong emotional intensity, and a lack of empathy. When people say they are “feeling triggered,” it’s likely that a complex was activated.

A complex distorts reality—it constricts and splinters the personality so the triggering event is viewed strictly through the lens of the complex. With the father complex, for example, men who lack emotions and dominate—those who emulate the patriarchal image of a man—are often viewed as more masculine, while those who do not can be devalued.

The “tradwife” movement is one example where we see the father complex play out. These “traditional wives” hold the belief that women should care for the household, while men should provide financially and make the family's decisions.

What Is the Father Complex?

As mentioned, the father complex organizes around power, authority, and authority figures. But it’s also related to themes such as achievement, compliance, rebellion, the masculine, paternity, and mistrust or fear of authority. The father complex is not solely shaped by one’s literal father—it also encompasses one's idea of “father,” what one did and did not experience with their father, as well as experiences with other authority figures and one's cultural upbringing.

Jungian analyst Mario Jacoby often emphasized that complexes have an autonomous quality and can “take over” the personality emotionally. A father complex may emerge in relationships with supervisors, professors, therapists, institutions, spiritual leaders, or romantic partners.

As with all complexes, the father complex has a bipolar structure, meaning it has two opposite sides with opposing tendencies within them: one more dominant and conscious, and the other less present and unconscious. Therefore, a positive father complex is not “purely positive.” Someone with a positive father complex may unexpectedly show rebellion, devaluation, and disappointment when authorities are human and let them down.

Someone with a positive father complex may view the father and authority positively. Some women may consider themselves a “daddy’s girl,” adopt a “father knows best” attitude, and apply this belief to authority in general. Authority may be idealized, creating a strong belief in and allegiance to a leader or authority figure. Women with a positive father complex may consciously feel that their father believed in them and that they can always count on him.

However, unconsciously, she may feel lovable mostly when she is achieving, may be critical of imperfections, and feel insecurity or fear about her own authority, especially if it differs from her father’s. Therefore, the positive father complex conceals the unconscious negative side she holds, such as toxic perfectionism or fear of her own autonomy.

Alternatively, someone with a negative father complex tends to have a negative conscious relationship to authority. They may rebel against authority figures. It may manifest as a struggle with achievement—perhaps moving from job to job. The bipolar structure means the conscious negative experience coexists with an unconscious positive pull to authority. While they may consciously feel critical, there is an often surprising, unconscious need to be embraced, seen, and valued by an authority figure.

The Link Between the Father Complex and “Tradwives”

Like the mother complex, the father complex is common. I had a patient who may be called a “tradwife” these days. She married her college sweetheart and became a stay-at-home mom. Her husband managed all finances and deposited money into an account she used for groceries and household items.

We started working together because she “stayed at home, exactly as I wanted, but home is not making me happy. What’s wrong with me?” Her emphasis on “home” was charged and pointed to the presence of a complex.

In sessions, my patient and I became curious about her father complex. What were her associations with “father,” “authority,” “achievement,” and “power”? How did these associations connect to “home”? We linked how those associations connected to patterns, and how these past influences showed up in the present. I tracked the charged reactions and sensations in her mind and body, and found ways to encourage reflection and engagement with her experience.

We worked with her tendency to feel overwhelmed as a stay-at-home mother. Exploring the “overwhelm” created space to understand that the way out was through. Her conflicted relationship to achievement led her to magnify stresses and become paralyzed. I helped her develop greater stress tolerance for the first time in her life. She wryly remarked that her father was her “rescuer,” and desired that from me. We explored how that made life easier in the moment, but diminished her confidence and competence to navigate stressors.

We explored how the familiarity and comfort of having an adoring father led her to easily succumb to her husband’s adoring gaze. We linked this to a fear of embracing her own authority and feeling objectified. Rather than creating an inner authority, she lacked autonomy, let others make decisions for her, and instead of a “happily ever after” narrative, she was miserable.

Complexes are not “gotten rid of.” We learn to live with them, but more consciously, so that instead of overwhelming us, we relate to and work with our complexes to make healthier choices. They are individualized, and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Engaging with this work not only helps one move forward with a mother and father complex, but also applies to a big topic in therapy: trauma. I’ll discuss the trauma complex in my next post.

item.title: Pausing for Effectiveness
item.description:
Leadership

Pausing for Effectiveness

Employ the power of the pause for gratitude, imagination, and curiosity.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Peter Drucker led by example in pausing before answering questions and in his presentations.
  • Pausing is useful in meetings, conversations with colleagues, and in planning and deliberations.
  • Intentional pauses can lead to insights, breakthroughs, and new knowledge.
  • We can be more effective by employing pauses in high-stakes, high-tension environments.
Source: Shutterstock

There is often pressure for leaders and other knowledge workers to continually act, speak, and perform. Sometimes those are the right strategies. But at other time, we need to slow down and pause.

Peter Drucker, the father of modern management, who died at age 95 in 2005, led by example. For instance, there were times when I interviewed him and he would not immediately answer a question. Instead, he'd take what seemed like a long pause, as he considered his answer.

He wasn’t doing it for dramatic effect. Instead, he was considering the most appropriate response. The pauses yielded better answers; they also added to his own considerable gravitas. He achieved the same effect while making presentations to large audiences, which added to a sense of spontaneity.

Many Dimensions of Pausing

Pausing is a multidimensional act. It can be useful during interviews and presentations, and also in meetings, conversations with colleagues, and in reviewing our own internal thoughts, planning, and deliberations. Since it seems natural to deliver thoughts and answers fast, pausing requires intention, to break the chain of relentless activity. Rushing to fill in conversational gaps, especially in situations such as negotiations and job interviews, can be counterproductive.

We can pause (whether alone or with others) for silence, gratitude, imagination, curiosity, wonder, awe, and appreciation. Some people use meditation and breathing techniques for this purpose. On a different level, we can pause for discovery through introspection and reflection, to take stock of life inside and outside the workplace. Drucker made a practice of doing so each July for many years, in between teaching semesters at the Drucker School of Management, at Claremont Graduate University in California; as he assessed the previous year and looked ahead to the next.

The Pause Principle: Kevin Cashman

Kevin Cashman, vice chairman, CEO and enterprise leader at the global consulting firm Korn Ferry, turns pausing into a manifesto for leaders in his book The Pause Principle: Step Back to Lead Forward. He writes that “The pause principle is the conscious, intentional process of stepping back, within ourselves and outside of ourselves, to lead forward with greater authenticity, purpose, and contribution.”

In Cashman’s view, intentional pausing, not just in meetings and conversations, but also in organizational and career planning and strategy, can lead to insights, breakthroughs, and new knowledge. Pauses can result in new ideas, especially through “questioning, listening, and synthesizing.”

The Pause Principle: Cynthia Kane

Cynthia Kane is CEO and founder of the Kane Intentional Communication Institute, LLC, and author of The Pause Principle: How to Keep Your Cool in Tough Situations. In an article in Leader to Leader, “How Leaders Can Apply the Pause Principle in Difficult Interactions,” she writes: “Pausing is not something we inherently know how to do or can do. It’s also not something others teach us how to do, especially in heated conversations.”

In attending to high-pressure situations, we should focus on “that split second between the other person’s words and our reaction.” Kane developed what she has termed the SOFTEN practices, which she explains are mindfulness-based. The practices bring awareness and effectiveness to anxiety-producing moments. In her words, they are: Sensation, Own the Discomfort, Focus on the Present, Take a Breath, Eyes Toward Another, Need to Say.

Pause on the Balcony: William Ury

William Ury is coauthor, with the late Roger Fisher, of the classic negotiation book Getting to Yes. He has negotiated in high-stakes, high-tension environments worldwide throughout his long career. In a Leader to Leader article, “How to Transform (Not Resolve) Conflict,” he writes that “Given just how hard it is to remember to pause in the heat of conflict, I have learned over the years to compensate by building something I call the balcony. The balcony is a place of calm and perspective where we can keep our eyes on the prize.”

In discussing various manifestations of the balcony concept, Ury notes that “building a balcony may simply mean designing a planned break—or series of breaks—in what may be a contentious meeting.” In its simplest terms, he believes that “we need to go to the balcony, not only to control our natural reactions, but to expand our perspective.”

Peter Drucker’s Productivity Paradoxes

Drucker also brought the power of the pause to productivity, a way to consider what our work is meant to accomplish. He advised asking the following three questions: "What is the task? What are we trying to accomplish? Why do it at all?" Similarly, he wrote often about “systematic abandonment”: If you were not already engaged in a particular activity, product, or service; knowing what you currently know, would you start doing it now, based on your experience and results?

Conclusion

There are ample opportunities each day to practice pausing. Some leaders have found value in asking for silence at the beginning of meetings, as a pause from what people have been doing and thinking prior to the meeting, preparation for approaching the agenda ahead.

We can intentionally pause to avoid impulsivity and rushing into unwise decisions and actions. Each day, we can try to become more aware of the possibilities of pausing, in our thoughts and our interactions, to become more effective leaders and human beings.

item.title: How to Cope While Waiting for a Diagnosis
item.description:
Anxiety

How to Cope While Waiting for a Diagnosis

What you can do to build resilience and decrease health anxiety.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Long specialist wait times can intensify health anxiety.
  • Sensitivity to anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty are top risk factors for health anxiety.
  • CBT, mindfulness, and exposure therapy are proven effective for treating health anxiety symptoms.

You are experiencing uncomfortable or painful symptoms you can’t explain, and they’re interfering with your life. Maybe your doctor has put in a referral for a specialist, but the earliest appointment is months away. For millions of us humans, this is our reality—and it’s a source of mounting anxiety and distress. It may feel like your life is “on hold,” and you are playing it safe until you get answers.

What is your mind doing while you wait for diagnostic clarity?

Maybe your mind fills the gaps with worst-case scenarios—not only do you imagine the worst possible thing wrong with you, but you worry that the delay is going to eliminate your medical options. Maybe you read a story or watched a documentary, or one of your relatives got diagnosed with something debilitating at a late stage, and by then it was too late.

You may become hyper-focused on symptoms, interpreting every sensation as a sign you are getting worse. The sense of helplessness can erode your trust in the healthcare system to understand your symptoms, and in your own mind to make sense of what is happening with your body.

Maybe you stop doing the things you know help you feel better (like exercise or socializing) and start doing things that contribute to hypervigilance and maybe even keep you up at night (excessive checking, reassurance-seeking, internet scouring).

Of course you are anxious! Anyone would be!

Health anxiety has become a problem when it is excessive, out of proportion with the realistic likelihood of having a serious medical problem, continues to be persistent despite negative test results and reassurance from doctors, or leads to significant distress and unhelpful behaviors that interfere with your ability to work, play, and love (Center for Clinical Interventions, ND).

How has waiting for care affected your thinking, your routines, or your sense of safety?

Risk Factors for Health Anxiety

A systematic review confirmed that anxiety sensitivity and intolerance of uncertainty are the two most frequently reported risk factors associated with health anxiety (Bükrük et al., 2026).

  • Intolerance of Uncertainty: Intolerance of uncertainty is the struggle to tolerate not knowing, and the drive to eliminate all ambiguity about health (Bükrük et al., 2026). Humans are wired to seek answers, especially when it comes to health. When our healthcare system can’t provide clarity, your brain’s threat response ramps up. The longer you wait, the more your mind tries to “solve” the problem, often by imagining the worst. For those with a history of trauma or chronic illness, the waiting period can reactivate old fears and deepen feelings of vulnerability. Intolerance of uncertainty drives the urge to seek absolute answers and certainty, fueling repeated checking, reassurance-seeking, and difficulty accepting “not knowing."
  • Anxiety Sensitivity: Anxiety sensitivity is the tendency to interpret normal bodily sensations as dangerous or catastrophic (Bükrük et al., 2026). Especially if you or others you know have had serious health issues in the past, accompanied by physical sensations, it is easy to see how our brains might treat the physical sensations themselves as dangerous. What physical sensations are the most scary for you? Stuff like heart racing or arrhythmia, shaking, sweaty palms/hot flashes, variable energy, painful joints, dizziness, irritability, tremors? Anxiety sensitivity leads to catastrophic interpretations of potentially normal or temporary uncomfortable bodily sensations, amplifying distress and health-focused behaviors.

What Increases Health Anxiety?

Unhelpful Thinking

  • Catastrophizing: “If my doctor is sending me to a specialist, it must be serious.”
  • Thinking the worst: “If I miss an important health symptom, it could kill me.”
  • All-or-nothing thinking: “I must have a diagnosis to move forward.”

Body Focus

  • Hypervigilance: Constantly scanning for new or changing symptoms.
  • Misinterpreting normal sensations as signs of severe illness.
  • Excessively monitoring bodily processes (pulse, blood pressure, weight). Don't know how much to monitor? Ask your doctor, and follow their advice.

Behaviors

  • Reassurance-seeking (asking family, friends, or doctors repeatedly for checkups).
  • Internet scouring for symptoms and worst-case scenarios.
  • Avoidance of activities or situations that might trigger symptoms to the point where life gets really small!
  • Withdrawing from enjoyable or meaningful activities.

What Helps: Skills for Thinking, Body, and Behavior

Thinking Skills

  • Name the Experience: Remind yourself: “I’m anxious because I don’t have answers yet.” Naming the feeling can reduce its grip.
  • Challenge Catastrophic Thoughts: Consider other possible explanations for your symptoms. Reflect on how you might cope if you got the news that most scares you. Have others been there before? How did they deal with it? What do you already know how to do when it comes to dealing with tough stuff?
  • Address Existential Themes: Diagnostic uncertainty can be a doorway to these themes.
    • Death: Facing mortality clarifies what matters most.
    • The Nature of Freedom: Awareness of lost choices highlights where agency remains.
    • Isolation: We are never fully understood by others—yet this aloneness is universal.
    • Meaning: There’s no ultimate guide to meaning; we must shape our own, integrating experience in ways that feel true and useful.

Body Skills

  • Ground in the Present: Use your senses to anchor yourself—what do you see, hear, feel, smell, or taste right now? Mindfulness and mundane task-focusing can retrain your attention away from symptoms.
  • Practice Relaxation or Mindfulness: Engage in breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided meditations to calm your nervous system.
  • Schedule “Worry Time”: Contain rumination by setting aside a specific time each day to write down or reflect on your worries, putting words to your body sensations, and freeing up the rest of your day for other experiences.

Behavior Skills

  • Limit Reassurance-Seeking: Notice when you’re Googling symptoms or seeking constant updates. Set gentle boundaries with yourself and gradually reduce these behaviors.
  • Practice Self-Advocacy: Ask for what you need, check for cancellations, seek interim support from your primary care provider, and recognize what’s within your control. Pair this with flexible health rules—such as, “If this pain worsens or persists another week, I’ll see the doctor."
  • Maintain Routines and Connection: Nourish your body, engage in activities that bring meaning or comfort, and connect with others. Share your experience with trusted friends, support groups, or a therapist.

What would it look like to continue to build resilience while waiting for a diagnosis?

Treating Health Anxiety

An analysis of 35 randomized controlled trials (3,263 participants) found the following interventions were effective for treating health anxiety: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, metacognitive therapy, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, and behavioral stress management (Lai et al., 2026). Specific elements of these therapies that helped the most included exposure and response prevention, cognitive restructuring, and mindfulness (ibid). Check out a free CBT for Health Anxiety protocol here, and consider finding a psychotherapist who specializes in treating health anxiety using one of these modalities.

If you’re caught in the uncertainty of waiting for specialist care, you can find ways to build resilience in your waiting.

item.title: 10 Things I've Learned as a Therapist
item.description:
Therapy

10 Things I've Learned as a Therapist

Personal Perspective: A good therapist learns from each session.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Therapy is a team effort.
  • Pay attention to the pace of therapy.
  • Listen with your eyes, ears, and feelings.
  • Don't jump to conclusions.

I have been on journeys with thousands of individuals for four decades. Yep; it's been four decades, and it's been quite a ride. Honestly, it has been an honor to be in my consulting room with individuals sharing their very personal histories and current struggles. I have always hoped that I am doing my very best guiding my patients. In the process, I have learned several life lessons that I would like to share as I continue my life's work. My hope is that this list will inform both therapists and patients alike. I will start with 10 of the most valuable lessons that inform my work. There will be a part 2 in the future.

  1. As a therapist, you are part of a team effort. You are not working in a vacuum. If you are working with children, you also work with the family. If you are working with an adult, you and the person in the chair opposite you are working together. This is hard work, and I remember a supervisor telling me that you should be sweating by the end of the session. I believe he was intending to convey that you should be totally present as a therapist.
  2. Individuals may present with similar presenting issues. Do not assume that they are reacting similarly and will benefit from the same set of skills. Everyone reacts and responds to situations differently. You must be aware that what may be easy for one person to understand and enact is difficult for another. Consider children who are being bullied. One child may be able to use his/her verbal skills to respond, while another child may need parental involvement. Try not to make the mistake that everyone is capable of everything that you may suggest.
  3. Do not judge a person's character too early. I have personally made this mistake, and I refer to this as a therapeutic error. Consider a woman who described marital problems. She described being a deeply religious woman and a loyal wife. As I got to know her, she revealed having a history of extramarital affairs with her daughter's male friends (men in their 20s). Her history was clearly more complicated than I initially assumed.
  4. Go into each session with the intention to learn something new. At the end of each session, there should be a takeaway for you and for your patient.
  5. Do not become complacent. This can occur when you assume that you know more than you actually do. It can also happen when you are not fully present.
  6. Jumping to conclusions about a person is problematic. You are on a journey with the patient. What you uncover after three months may be considerably more helpful and complicated than what you learn after one month. I have worked with several individuals who divulged adverse childhood experiences only after several months. Issues such as being molested and/or abused usually do not get discussed early on in therapy.
  7. Develop a trusting connection. Nothing good will happen in therapy if your patient finds you judgmental and lacking authentic empathy. If you lack empathy for a patient, perhaps you are the wrong therapist.
  8. Pay attention to the pace. Do not proceed too quickly. Always try to pay attention to when the patient is ready to answer specific questions. Consider, for example, that early in therapy, a patient may not be ready to tell you that she has been checking her partner's phone.
  9. Listen with your eyes, ears, and feelings. What you, as a therapist, are feeling may be how the patient or those around the patient may be feeling. If you feel unusually frustrated in session, assess whether or not your patient is also feeling frustrated. This is invaluable information.
  10. Focus on strengths as well as areas that require improvement. Provide balance in therapy. No one wants to be seen only as a set of issues that need improvement.

item.title: How to Dismantle Self-Criticism in the Face of Chronic Illness
item.description:
Chronic Illness

How to Dismantle Self-Criticism in the Face of Chronic Illness

Learn to understand and modify self-attacks.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Self-criticism in chronic illness often stems from emotions like shame, anger, and sadness.
  • Modifying self-criticism involves enlisting healthy parts of the self to challenge negative self-talk.
  • Cultivating self-protection and self-compassion counters the damage of self-criticism.
Source: Katie Willard Virant

Living with chronic illness is hard. Symptoms can affect our ability to do seemingly simple tasks. They also can be embarrassing and difficult to talk about. In short, chronic illness can make us feel diminished, angry, sad, and ashamed.

Sometimes, people living with chronic illness take all of these challenging emotions and turn them against themselves (Trindade et al., 2019). For example, a woman living with multiple sclerosis berates herself when she loses her balance, calling herself "stupid and weak." A man living with IBD isolates from friends, thinking, “I’m no fun to be around.” A person with rheumatoid arthritis blames themselves for not being “a good patient” who can accept their diagnosis with equanimity.

This post examines the way self-criticism manifests in chronic illness. We will try to understand it together and look at ways to modify it.

When Self-Criticism Is Helpful—and When It Isn't

I want to differentiate helpful from harmful self-criticism (Sokova, 2025). Helpful self-criticism—which I would label “quest for self-improvement”—identifies places where we can improve our quality of life, set attainable goals toward that end, and implement changes that move us toward those goals. When we pursue self-improvement, we often feel purposeful and empowered. We are identifying issues within our control, making a plan that feels do-able, and acting accordingly.

By contrast, self-criticism that is detrimental does not feel empowering or purposeful. Rather, it feels depleting, frustrating, and shaming. Someone working to self-improve may say, “I would feel better with more exercise, even though my illness makes that challenging. I will start by walking for 10 minutes three times a week.” Someone inclined to self-criticism will say, “I am so lazy that I could never make an exercise program work. Even if I try a little bit, it’s a drop in the bucket. It’s pathetic that I am this weak. I’d be embarrassed for people to see me struggling with this.”

Types of Self-Criticism

Self-criticism is harsh. It blames the self for things beyond the self’s control; it sits in judgment of the self’s abilities and efforts; and it tells the self that change is futile. Self-criticism is strongly linked with depression, anxiety, and other mental illness diagnoses (Kannan & Levitt, 2013). Self-criticism presents in two main ways: the inadequate self and the hated self (Sokova, 2025).

The inadequate self is experienced as a flawed, damaged self who cannot do anything right. There’s a profound disappointment in that self; a belief that it is shameful. The hated self is experienced with anger and a wish to destroy. The self is seen as so bad that it needs to be punished or eradicated. Either or both of these experiences of self can occur in a person who is self-critical.

How to Modify Self-Criticism

The first step in changing self-critical patterns in chronic illness is to understand how and when self-criticism shows up for you. Keep a record for a week or so of self-critical thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Write down how they show up (e.g., negative self-talk, deflated and/or angry feelings, behaviors like self-isolating or self-harming) and when they appear (e.g., what events cause them to arise).

When you have completed your log, see if you can find patterns. Maybe you notice that a particular type of experience makes you furious at yourself and another makes you feel deflated. For example, you may find that an increase in chronic illness fatigue causes you to berate yourself as lazy and worthless, while interactions with others spark a shameful feeling that your illness makes you unlikeable.

Once you’ve identified these patterns, try to identify them as a part of you, rather than as the whole of “who you are”. It may be helpful to name this critical part as “my critical self,” “the critical part of me,” or “the critical voice inside.” This is a helpful practice, as you now have two parts of yourself online—the critical self and the neutral, observing self.

Work with your neutral, observing self to be curious about your self-criticism. Evaluate the statements made by your critical voice. Are they true, or do they just feel true? Your neutral self can observe that feelings are not facts and that you are likely not the horrible failure that your critical self claims you to be. Your critical voice is also likely to be overly dramatic, making broad statements like “You will never amount to anything!” or “One mistake means that you are a loser!” Let your neutral, observing self notice and challenge that hyperbole.

Next, we’re going to bring another part of self online: the self-protective part. This part steps in to protect the self from the damage caused by self-criticism, saying: “I don’t deserve this, and you need to stop. I would not accept these judgments if you were saying them to someone I love, and I will not accept them about myself.”

Ready for the next part we’re going to enlist? This is the self-compassionate part of self. Once we’ve told the self-criticism to stand down, we’re going to move in to tend to ourselves. We’re going to say, “It is hard living with chronic illness. It brings up lots of feelings, including sorrow, grief, anger, and fear. But I don’t have to berate, judge, and criticize myself. I can feel my feelings without turning them into an attack against myself.”

Conclusion

Modifying self-criticism is challenging and important work. Hopefully, this has given you an overview of the process. Remember that therapists are trained to help you with this work. It’s beneficial to seek assistance, especially if you have difficulty finding and using your self-protective and self-compassionate parts of self. Understanding and treating self-criticism is vital in improving quality of life with chronic illness.

item.title: What VHS Rewind Time Reveals About Screen Time
item.description:
Media

What VHS Rewind Time Reveals About Screen Time

Personal Perspective: Sometimes the value of media lies in the pauses.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Screen time is too broad a category to be labeled simply good or bad.
  • Media effects depend on what people are doing, using, and potentially replacing.
  • Older technologies often created pauses that streaming platforms now remove.
  • Intentional breaks can create space for conversation, creativity, and connection.

A few months ago, I bought a TV/VCR combo for $50 from an older gentleman on Facebook Marketplace. He told me it hadn't been turned on in more than 15 years.

Against all odds, it worked. Mostly. The built-in VCR occasionally gets stuck, and I have to use a small tool to manually eject tapes. But I make it work.

Since then, I've slowly built a VHS collection from thrift stores and antique malls, never spending more than $2-3 per tape.

At first, the television was mostly a fun nostalgia and novelty project. The DVD player launched in the U.S. when I was less than a year old, so admittedly, I only remember using VHS tapes at my grandma's house until she, too, transitioned to DVD.

But as a communication and technology scholar, I started noticing something interesting.

For several weeks, I watched a movie before going to sleep. During that time, I found myself putting my phone down one to two hours before falling asleep and, ultimately, sleeping better. The experience felt slower and more intentional, although I know there is a lot to be said about not having a television in your bedroom.

Then I moved, and the television ended up sitting in my garage collecting dust.

A few months later, my best friend and her 11-year-old daughter came to visit.

Knowing they were coming, I had intentionally collected several Mary-Kate & Ashley VHS tapes. We pulled the television out of storage, dusted it off, and settled in for a movie marathon.

That is when I found myself watching something happen in real time that perfectly illustrated a concept I often teach.

The Screen Time Question We Keep Asking

When people talk about technology and well-being, the conversation often centers on a single question:

Is screen time good or bad?

Parents worry about it, schools debate it, and news headlines warn about it.

But as a researcher, I have never found that question particularly useful.

Screen time is not one single thing. Watching a movie with people you love is different from doomscrolling alone. Video chatting with a grandparent is different from being pulled into autoplay for hours. Playing a creative game is different from using technology to compare, bully, or disconnect.

Research supports this more complicated picture. Orben and Przybylski (2019), for example, found that associations between digital technology use and adolescent well-being were small and difficult to interpret. More recent diary research adds another layer: different platforms may have different effects. Van der Wal and colleagues (2026) analyzed more than 44,000 daily diaries from 479 adolescents and found that social media use could affect well-being, self-esteem, and friendship closeness differently, with some platforms showing more negative associations than others.

That is why the better question is not simply how much time we spend with screens.

It is what we are doing with that time, how it fits into the rest of our lives, and what it may be replacing.

That is what the VHS reminded me of.

The Unexpected Value of Rewind Time

Before we could even start our movie marathon, we had to wait for the first tape to rewind.

For anyone who grew up with streaming services, that sentence probably sounds ridiculous.

After the first movie, I got up to switch the tapes. We were ready for the next one to begin, having already taken a quick bathroom and snack break. As we settled back into our movie marathon, we were struck by the realization:

We had to wait.

Again.

Because rewinding a VHS tape takes time. A surprising amount of time.

The first rewind, we talked about how people used to watch movies and why “be kind and rewind” was such a popular phrase. By the third rewind, we had settled into a rhythm.

We colored.

We crafted.

We talked.

At one point, we even started another movie that was only available through streaming. For a while, the VHS tape was rewinding on a television to our right while a movie played on a flatscreen directly in front of us.

As I sat there, I saw two completely different philosophies of media.

One was built around waiting.

The other was built around immediacy.

The VHS was not a better technology. It was, and is, objectively less convenient.

But that inconvenience created something modern media often removes:

A pause.

What Happens When We Remove Every Pause?

Streaming platforms are designed to keep us watching.

Autoplay starts the next episode. Recommendations appear instantly. Entire seasons are available with a single click.

These features make media consumption seamless, which is often exactly what we want. And honestly, who doesn't love a good binge-watching session?

But they also eliminate many of the natural stopping points where communication and relationship maintenance can happen.

Having to wait for a tape to rewind created those stopping points for us. It gave us a reason to look away from the screen, pick up something else, and settle into a different kind of shared time.

In my previous post on soft socializing, I wrote about how connection does not always require deep conversation or constant engagement. Sometimes, relationships are built through shared activities, parallel play, and low-pressure time together.

Rewind time created that kind of space almost accidentally. It gave us something to do, but not too much to do. It allowed us to be together without needing to perform togetherness.

That is part of why the moment stayed with me.

Bringing Back the Rewind Break

I am not suggesting that families abandon streaming services and return to VHS tapes.

I am certainly not giving up the convenience of streaming (how else would I watch Love Island or Heated Rivalry?)

But I do think there is something worth learning from rewind time.

We can create pauses even when technology no longer requires them. Here are a few ways to do so:

  • Finish an episode and spend 15 minutes coloring.
  • Take a walk before starting the next movie.
  • Make a snack together.
  • Talk.
  • Or simply sit in the same room for a few minutes before pressing play again.

The goal is not necessarily less screen time, but instead, creating more opportunities for everything else, too.

At the end of the visit, even after the rewind time, the 11-year-old told me she wanted a TV/VCR combo when she grew up. She said, "I want a 'big girl TV', just like you."

I laughed, but I also understood why.

The appeal was not just the movies. It was the whole experience: the tapes, the waiting, the crafting, the talking, and the little pauses that made the movie marathon feel like more than just watching movies.

Maybe that is what rewind time reminded me of most...Sometimes the best part of technology is not what happens on the screen, but it is what has room to happen around it.

item.title: Why Am I So Exhausted When I’m Doing Everything “Right”?
item.description:
Burnout

Why Am I So Exhausted When I’m Doing Everything “Right”?

The hidden cost of identity fatigue.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Exhaustion may be caused by identity fatigue, not simply doing too much or lack of rest.
  • Overthinking can become a learned identity, not just a habit.
  • Repeated self-suppression carries a physiological cost, wearing down the body's adaptive systems over time.
  • Recovery is not more strategies, but attuning to what the body and deeper self are trying to communicate.

“I’m utterly exhausted most of the time. When I wake up my head feels heavy and my body feels sluggish. I can’t think clearly. Before the day has even started, I’m worried I won’t be able to function properly at work, worried I’ll get found out, or worse... lose my job.”

A client said this to me recently, and I suspect many people can empathise with the experience.

This is not the tiredness that comes after a late night, a tough week, or too much physical exertion. This is something more persistent – a kind of debilitating depletion. You sleep, but don’t feel restored. You listen to advice on podcasts, dial in your nutrition, monitor your sleep and movement metrics, and stick to a morning routine, yet you still feel wiped out.

In the absence of a diagnosed medical, hormonal, or sleep-related condition, this kind of exhaustion often sits within a broader mind-body context. But that phrase can be vague. What does it actually mean?

We live in a culture that is more educated and informed than ever before. Health, well-being, and personal development advice is freely available and easily accessible. For most problems or challenges experienced, there are protocols, techniques, supplements, apps, or productivity hacks. In 2026, AI may be the first place people turn for help. It will offer useful suggestions on sleep hygiene, movement, nutrition, and nervous system regulation — all of which are sensible and valid.

But for many experiencing persistent fatigue and exhaustion, something is missing.

We often treat exhaustion as the result of doing too much. But sometimes the deeper issue is the hidden effort of being someone we learned to be. I think of this as identity fatigue: the exhaustion that comes from repeatedly performing a version of yourself — a version that once helped you adapt, belong, succeed, or stay safe, but now requires you to override too much of who you are beneath the protective layers. It's the tiredness that comes from having to be capable, agreeable, productive, and a peacemaker — the one who keeps going and doesn't disappoint. These identities may have served an important purpose. But when they become fixed, they can quietly drain the life from us.

For some people, identity fatigue shows up as living almost entirely in the mind. Thinking began as the place they would retreat to when the body felt too uncertain, unsafe, and emotionally overwhelmed. But over time, the thinking mind became a place of permanent residence, and a constructed identity emerged.

Analysis, mental rehearsal, monitoring, predicting, planning, and scanning can become continuous activities, often running at the edge of awareness. What began as an intelligent protective strategy can become an unconscious pattern on autopilot, especially for those who learned early in life that inhabiting the body or being fully themselves did not feel safe. Eventually, the thinking self can form its own identity. “This is just who I am,” we often say. “I live in my head and overthink.” “I need to understand everything.” “I can’t switch off.” Yet what looks like personality may actually be a survival strategy that is depleting the system.

This is not merely psychological in nature. The body pays a physiological price for enduring ongoing pressure, threat, and emotional demand. Research on stress and allostatic load suggests that when a body repeatedly adapts to pressure, uncertainty, and emotional demand, its regulatory systems get worn down. The body works hard to protect and mobilise us in the face of these perceived dangers, but the cost of that sustained effort accumulates over time.

If the deeper problem is disconnection, more thought and more control can become additional hidden causes. Seeking external fixes, like stricter routines, productivity hacks, and wellness protocols, all become more attempts to force the body to feel more energised.

The body often notices identity fatigue before the mind does. You may tell yourself you are simply being responsible, professional, helpful, considerate, or reasonable. But the body may register the performance differently: a tight chest when you say "yes" again, heaviness before another important meeting, shallow breathing around certain people, resentment after being “fine” all day, or numbness after too much self-suppression. These signals are not random. They may be signs that a learned identity is running the show.

The question, then, is not simply, “How do I get more energy?” but “Which version of me is depleting my energy?” Is it the capable self that cannot admit it is struggling? The agreeable self that says "yes" before checking what feels right? The monitoring self that tries to solve every sensation, feeling, and uncertainty with more thinking? The peacemaker who keeps everyone else comfortable while suppressing true feelings?

If this resonates, you could pose some deeper questions to yourself:

“What am I having to suppress in order to keep going?”

“What part of me am I leaving behind in order to function?”

“Where am I living from fear rather than alignment?”

“What does my body know that my mind keeps trying to override?”

“What might happen if I let my real self out?”

“Who am I underneath the chattering mind?”

When we begin to notice that we are living from the mind and the learned self, we can gently redirect attention to the body, emotions, needs, and values. Exhaustion may then begin to soften and energy return, not because life has changed, but because the version of us meeting life has changed.

In practical terms, the change does not need to be dramatic. In fact, in many instances, it may require doing less, not more. It might mean pausing for thirty seconds before agreeing to take on another task at work; saying nothing rather than trying to manage or fix someone else’s emotions; allowing yourself to say what you really feel; noticing when tension appears in the body without ignoring or dismissing it; or allowing emotion to be felt rather than suppressed or explained away. It may require creating a gap between the situation and action, and feeling what really matters to you now, rather than what used to matter in the past, or what matters to other people.

Over time, these small changes make a big difference. We rarely think our way out of a mind-generated identity; more often, we have to feel our way through it one step at a time. These small moments interrupt the automatic patterns that have hijacked how we present ourselves to the world. They create a gap between the learned self and the deeper self. And in that gap, energy can begin to return — not through more thinking, control, or force, but through the gradual return of flow.
